Economics
December 2012
# Economic Focus **Building a recovery** There has been a rapid rise in US house building through 2012, and the last few months in particular. During October, construction started on 888,000 new houses (annualised rate), the highest number since July 2008 and up by 41% from October 2011. Although this recovery in housing is built upon solid foundations, it is questionable whether such a pace of recovery can be sustained through 2013 or make a large impact on headline economic growth. House building is recovering from an extremely low base; the latest figures are still 60% below the 2006 peak. That low base is a critical factor behind the recovery. From 1980 to 2000, house building in the US averaged close to 1.5 million units per year. And although the rate peaked at over 2 million during the bubble of the past decade, since the start of 2008 it has averaged less than 700,000 units. In short, under-building in the past few years has been much greater than overbuilding during the bubble. Housing supply has failed to keep pace with continued growth in the US population of around 3 million people per year. In many areas, the excess supply of housing following the collapse of the bubble is gone, and the market has become quite tight. The fundamental demand for more house building is strong. **Household finances a concern** However, all is not well with the US housing market, and several factors suggest the pace of recovery may not last. By splitting the housing starts data into single-family units (houses) and multi-family units (apartments), we can see that growth is significantly faster in apartments building. Foreclosures have pushed former homeowners into the rental market, while potential first time buyers are also forced into renting due to a restrictive Economic Focus mortgage market. The resulting increase in rents has made it quite lucrative for developers to build new apartments for the rental market, where mortgage lending restrictions are less of an issue. But apartment building is now drawing closer to historical trend levels. If a strong recovery in housing starts is to continue, it must increasingly come from actual houses. Mortgage activity remains low Arguably, the recovery in building single-family houses is being held back by the credit
markets. The US Federal Reserve has begun to address the issue; back in September it commenced buying mortgage-
backed securities in an attempt to drive down mortgage rates. The move appears to have had some success – mortgage
rates are at record lows, with the effective rate on a 30-year fixed rate mortgage currently around 3.6%. As of yet,
however, this has not resulted in a sharp rise in lending. Mortgage applications for the purchase of single-family homes
(see chart above) remain depressed. Fed Chairman Bernanke said last month that “overly tight lending standards may
now be preventing credit worthy borrowers from buying homes”. With many lenders still dealing with the fallout from the
housing bubble, it is unlikely that lending standards will ease significantly during the coming year.

**Mortgage activity remains low** Arguably, the recovery in building single-family houses is being held back by the credit markets. The US Federal Reserve has begun to address the issue; back in September it commenced buying mortgagebacked securities in an attempt to drive down mortgage rates. The move appears to have had some success – mortgage rates are at record lows, with the effective rate on a 30-year fixed rate mortgage currently around 3.6%. As of yet, however, this has not resulted in a sharp rise in lending. Mortgage applications for the purchase of single-family homes (see chart above) remain depressed. Fed Chairman Bernanke said last month that “overly tight lending standards may now be preventing credit worthy borrowers from buying homes”. With many lenders still dealing with the fallout from the housing bubble, it is unlikely that lending standards will ease significantly during the coming year. **Slower growth for 2013** Wood Mackenzie expects the recovery in house building to continue through 2013, but the pace of growth is unlikely to match the 27% year on year growth we have seen in 2012 to date. We forecast a further Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2012 Page 2 of 6 Economic Focus 13% growth in housing starts, supported by pent-up demand but constrained by lending conditions. While a recovery in US housing is a positive for the wider economy, it is important not to overstate its impact. Housing investment accounts for just 2.7% of GDP at present, compared with a peak of ~6% in 2005. Perhaps more important is how the housing market in

teracts with other key drivers of the economy, specifically consumption. Although house building is increasing in the US, house prices are at best rising slowly. As such, they are unlikely to trigger a rapid rise in household consumption via the wealth effect.
